23377:
A prophet was called by God to speak his word, often beginning with "Thus says the LORD." Prophets confronted kings, called Israel back to covenant faithfulness, announced judgment and promised restoration. They were called individually, not by heredity; Amos insisted he was a herdsman, not a professional prophet.

Deuteronomy gives tests for prophets and promises a prophet like Moses, a promise the New Testament applies to Jesus. Women prophets include Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Anna and Philip's daughters. In the church, prophecy is listed among spiritual gifts; whether it continues today is debated between continuationists and cessationists.
23383: God will raise up a prophet like Moses; Peter applies this to Jesus.
23384: God spoke through the prophets in many ways, but finally through his Son.
23385: Prophets spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
23386: A prophet is not without honour except in his hometown.
23387: Church prophecy is to be weighed by others and done in order.
23389:
In the book of Judges, a *shofet* was less a courtroom official than a God-raised deliverer and leader who rescued tribes from oppression and then governed. Some, like Deborah, also settled disputes. The book follows a repeating cycle of sin, oppression, crying out and deliverance, and the judges themselves grow morally weaker as it goes on.

More broadly, the law required judges to be appointed in every town to judge impartially and refuse bribes. Eli and Samuel judged Israel before the monarchy.
23390: Seat at the city gate or under a palm
23392: The parable of the unjust judge contrasts a reluctant judge with a God who answers prayer.
23393: There is one lawgiver and judge; believers must not judge one another hypocritically.
23394: The Father has given all judgment to the Son, appointed judge of the living and the dead.
23395:
Israel asked for a king "like all the nations," which Samuel saw as rejecting God's kingship. Deuteronomy's law of the king forbids multiplying horses, wives and silver and requires the king to copy and read the law. Kings were anointed with oil, making them "the LORD's anointed."

God's covenant with David promised an enduring dynasty, the root of messianic hope. The books of Kings evaluate each ruler by covenant faithfulness, especially in worship. The Gospels present Jesus as the Son of David and King of the Jews, whose kingdom is not from this world.
23402: The LORD's anointed king will rule the nations, a psalm the New Testament applies to Jesus.
23403: The ideal king defends the poor and needy.
23404: Jesus tells Pilate his kingdom is not from this world.
23405: Christ is King of kings and Lord of lords.
23406: Parables of a king's wedding feast and a king settling accounts picture God's reign.
23407:
An apostle (Greek *apostolos*, "one sent") was a commissioned messenger. Jesus chose twelve to be with him and to be sent out, a number echoing Israel's twelve tribes. After Judas' death, Matthias was chosen, the criterion being a witness of Jesus' ministry and resurrection.

Paul claimed apostleship by a direct commission from the risen Christ. The word also applies more broadly to others such as Barnabas, and possibly to Andronicus and Junia (the reading of Romans 16:7 is debated). Traditions disagree about whether apostolic authority continues: Catholic and Orthodox churches teach apostolic succession through bishops; most Protestants hold that the foundational apostolic office ended with the first generation.
23412: The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone.
23413: Jesus himself is called the apostle and high priest of our confession.
23414: Paul lists appearances of the risen Jesus, last of all to him as one untimely born.
23415: Apostles are presented as servants who suffer, not as celebrities.
23417:
An evangelist (*euangelistēs*) is one who announces good news. The word occurs only three times in the New Testament: of Philip, one of the Seven, who preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official; in Ephesians' list of ministries Christ gives the church; and in Paul's charge to Timothy to "do the work of an evangelist."

In later usage "the Evangelists" also means the four Gospel writers.
23421: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.
23422: Philip explains Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian, beginning from that scripture to tell him the good news of Jesus.
23423: Scattered believers preached the word wherever they went.
23425:
"Pastor" comes from the Latin for shepherd and translates the Greek *poimēn* in Ephesians 4:11, the only place the noun is used for a church role. The verb "to shepherd" is used of elders, who are told to shepherd God's flock willingly and by example under Christ, the chief Shepherd.

Whether pastors, elders and overseers are one office described by different terms, and whether "pastors and teachers" in Ephesians names one role or two, is debated.
23429: Jesus commissions Peter to feed and tend his sheep.
23430: Paul tells the Ephesian elders to shepherd the church of God, bought with his own blood, and to watch for wolves.
23431: God promises shepherds after his own heart and condemns those who scatter the flock.
23432: Christ is the great Shepherd of the sheep and the chief Shepherd.
23434:
Teaching God's law was a duty of parents, priests and Levites, and Ezra set his heart to study, do and teach it. In Jesus' day teachers of the law were addressed as "rabbi"; Jesus himself was called Rabbi and Teacher, and Gamaliel was a respected teacher under whom Paul trained.

In the church, teachers are listed among Christ's gifts. Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God more accurately to Apollos, and teachers served alongside prophets at Antioch. James warns that teachers will be judged more strictly.
23438: Parents are to teach God's words diligently to their children.
23439: The Great Commission includes teaching disciples to obey all Jesus commanded.
23440: Not many should become teachers, since teachers face stricter judgment.
23441: Timothy is to entrust teaching to faithful people who can teach others.
23442: Jesus warns against seeking the title rabbi, for one is the Teacher.
23444:
In Israel, elders were senior heads of families and clans who represented the people, sat at the city gate to decide cases and witnessed transactions. Moses appointed seventy elders to share his burden.

The early churches were led by groups of elders (*presbyteroi*). In Acts 20 and Titus 1 the same people are called elders and overseers (*episkopoi*), so many conclude the terms were interchangeable at first. Qualifications focus on character, family life and ability to teach. By the early second century, Ignatius of Antioch describes a single bishop over elders and deacons; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches see this as legitimate development, while Presbyterian and many free churches favour plural elder leadership.
23447: Prayer and anointing of the sick
23448: Elders are to shepherd willingly, not for gain, as examples to the flock.
23449: The sick may call the elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil.
23450: The twenty-four elders around the throne lead heavenly worship.
23451:
*Diakonos* means servant or minister and is used broadly of anyone who serves, including Christ, Paul and even civil rulers. It also became a title for a recognised church role: Paul greets "overseers and deacons" at Philippi, and 1 Timothy lists deacons' qualifications.

Many trace the role to the Seven chosen in Acts 6 to oversee the daily food distribution so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the word. Acts does not call them deacons, though it uses the related noun and verb for their service, so the link is a common reading rather than explicit. Two of the Seven, Stephen and Philip, are later seen preaching.
23453: Care for widows and the poor
23454: Whoever would be great must be servant (diakonos) of all, as the Son of Man came to serve.
23455: Deacons must be dignified, not greedy, holding the faith with a clear conscience, and first tested.
23456: Paul and Apollos are only servants through whom the Corinthians believed.
23458:
Paul commends Phoebe as a *diakonos* of the church at Cenchreae and a *prostatis* (patron or benefactor) of many, including himself; she probably carried the letter to Rome. Whether *diakonos* here names an office ("deacon" or "deaconess") or means "servant" in a general sense is debated, as is whether "the women" in 1 Timothy 3:11 are deacons' wives or women deacons.

Outside scripture, Pliny the Younger (about AD 112) reports interrogating two slave women called *ministrae*, likely a Latin rendering of deacons. Later church orders and councils describe an order of deaconesses who assisted at the baptism of women and ministered to women; the order faded in the West in the Middle Ages. Views today range from recognising women deacons as an ordained office, to seeing a non-ordained women's ministry, to reading Phoebe simply as a faithful servant.
23462: Paul asks the Romans to welcome Phoebe in the Lord and help her in whatever she needs.
23463: "Women likewise" in the deacons' qualifications is read either as wives of deacons or as women deacons.
23464: Enrolled widows of good works may represent another recognised women's ministry.
23466:
A Nazirite (from Hebrew *nazir*, "consecrated" or "separated") took a vow of special dedication to God for a set period. The law required three things: no wine, grapes or anything from the vine; no razor on the head; and no contact with a corpse, even of a close relative. At the end, the hair was shaved and offered with sacrifices. Anyone, man or woman, could take the vow.

Samson was a Nazirite from birth by divine command, and Hannah vowed that no razor would touch Samuel's head. Luke says John the Baptist would drink no wine, which many read as Nazirite-like. Paul cut his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow, and in Jerusalem paid the expenses of men completing a vow. "Nazarene" (from Nazareth) is a different word.
23470: Samson's broken consecration and recovered strength show that his power lay in God, not his hair as such.
23471: God raised up Nazirites and prophets, and Israel corrupted both.
23472: Jesus, unlike John, came eating and drinking, so the Nazirite pattern was not his.
